Who we are

Two homelands,
one roar.

The Princeton Bengal Tigers bring together students of Bengali heritage — from Bangladesh, West Bengal, and everywhere the diaspora has carried us — along with everyone curious enough to pull up a chair and share a plate of biryani.

Why "Bengal Tigers"? The Royal Bengal tiger is the national animal of Bangladesh — and, by a happy coincidence, Princeton's mascot too. Two flags, one fierce cat. We couldn't have written it better ourselves.

The language
we carry.

On 21 February 1952, students in Dhaka gave their lives for the right to speak their mother tongue. That day became Ekushey February, and later International Mother Language Day, honored across the world by UNESCO. The Shohid Minar stands in their memory. Every February we gather to raise it again — thousands of miles from home, in our own words.

In our own words

We handed members a whiteboard and one question: what does your mother tongue mean to you?

In her words

She drew the monument itself

Asked what her language means to her, she sketched the Shohid Minar — the memory the whole day is built around.

In his words

On speaking Bangla, far from home

A note on why he still chooses his mother tongue, an ocean away from where he first learned it.

On campus

Where home follows you.

Iftar dinners and Pohela Boishakh feasts. Late-night adda that runs past every problem set. A lot of dancing. This is what belonging looks like.

The year in celebration

Come celebrate with us

Our calendar follows the Bengali one — from the first day of Boishakh to the longest night of December. Everyone's invited; no experience with luchi required.

🕯️

Ekushey February

আন্তর্জাতিক মাতৃভাষা দিবস

Candlelight, poetry, and the Shohid Minar. We mark International Mother Language Day the way it was meant to be marked.

🌸
Mid-April

Pohela Boishakh

শুভ নববর্ষ

Bengali New Year in full color — panta bhat, music, and enough food to feed all of campus. Our biggest party of the year.

Community Iftar
